articles.title: Pediatric palliative care addresses the unique needs of seriously ill children and their families
articles.author: Khaliah Johnson, Associate Professor of Pediatrics, Emory University
paras: Pediatric medicine generally entails caring for patients at the beginning of their lives – performing newborn checkups, treating childhood illnesses and supporting adolescents in their health as they move toward adulthood.
So people are often surprised to hear about specialists like us who work in pediatric palliative care, helping children facing serious illness who may be nearing the end of their lives.

This approach to care focuses on relieving suffering and addressing quality of life for children and families facing complex, life-limiting medical conditions. We also work to ensure that every family who needs it has access to this care, because right now, these programs aren’t available to most families globally who need them.
Pediatric palliative care is an approach that emerged out of the adult hospice and palliative care movement in the 1990s to early 2000s as a distinct discipline.

Globally, an estimated 7 million children die annually. Children with life-threatening health conditions often live longer between the time of diagnosis and death than adults. They benefit from approaches to care that consider the needs of their caregivers and family members.

Pediatric palliative care is provided by a team of professionals, including physicians, nurses, social workers, child life specialists, chaplains and other allied health professionals who take a comprehensive approach to a child’s care as they live with serious illness and ultimately approach the end of their life. The goal of this care is to support families in making every day as good as it possibly can be, regardless of whether or not a child’s life remaining is short. At the heart of this approach is the belief that each child has a right to holistic, empathetic care during illness and throughout end of their life that considers their unique social, cultural, physical and spiritual needs.

For example, an infant who is diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder that affects vital organ function and shortens life expectancy may need to be in and out of the hospital to manage acute illnesses and complex symptoms, such as pain and difficulty breathing. In turn, her parents may need help with deciding which treatments will be most helpful or may cause more suffering than benefit.

A palliative care team works with patients and caregivers to formulate a plan that ensures this baby gets care that affords her opportunities to experience as many happy moments as possible. This can improve the lived experience of this child and her parents.

Children and families who have benefited from pediatric palliative care describe these services as the supportive lifeline that helped them to navigate the complexities of diagnosis, life with serious illness and, ultimately, death and bereavement.

Over the past 20 years, there has been growing evidence suggesting the benefits of this approach. Children who receive care from pediatric palliative care specialists have less pain, nausea and other distressing symptoms that can affect their day-to-day function and overall quality of life.

Research also shows that children admitted to intensive care settings for managing life-threatening illness are more likely to receive care that aligns with their goals. When a palliative care specialist is consulted, patients are less likely to opt for life-sustaining therapies that would not change their long-term prognosis.
The US on the cutting edge

The U.S. is on the global forefront of pediatric palliative care: Nearly 80% of U.S. children’s hospitals have formal, interdisciplinary programs to provide this specialized care. But access to services in a clinic setting or at home is less consistent. Not every hospital-based palliative care program is connected to outpatient or home-based services, creating gaps for patients and families who need to access this supportive care between hospitalizations.

Generally, palliative care in the U.S. is more readily available in urban settings and at academic medical centers than in rural areas and community hospitals. These differences are most pronounced in rural states and the Southeast, a region of the country that has historically had health disparities across racial and socioeconomic differences. It can be difficult for children in these places to access patient-centered, interdisciplinary supportive services.

Outside the U.S., pediatric palliative care can be even more difficult to access. Though it’s hard to measure, estimates suggest that more than 21 million children worldwide would benefit from a pediatric palliative care approach.

More than half of the world’s population live in countries where the availability of any palliative care is defined as either emerging or progressing, according to the World Health Organization. Only 14% of countries – 28 total – are considered to have advanced levels of palliative care development. The numbers are fairly similar for pediatrics, with one study identifying only 11 countries as reaching the highest level of pediatric palliative care development.

As many as 97% of children in need of this approach live in low- and middle-income countries. Children in these countries have less access to medical diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and are often diagnosed at later stages of illness with less access to curative therapy.

The types of pediatric serious illnesses seen in the developing world are also very different from the landscape in the U.S. The greatest need for pediatric palliative care in developing nations – about 30% of cases – is in children with HIV. Among other children needing palliative care, about 18% are living with complications from prematurity, roughly 16% suffer from congenital malformations, and about 16% are dealing with injuries leading to severe neurologic impairment.

In contrast to many high-income settings, children with malignant diseases such as leukemias and solid tumors represent a relatively small proportion – about 4% – of patients who would benefit from a palliative care approach. In these regions, the predominant ailments are HIV/AIDS, premature birth and birth trauma, congenital anomalies and injuries.

In low- and middle-income countries, essential medications like morphine, used for controlling pain and other symptoms, often aren’t available. In addition, healthcare workers often haven’t been trained in foundational principles of palliative care.
On top of that, many of these countries don’t have the political infrastructure to provide basic healthcare, much less facilitate developing a comprehensive palliative care program for children.

The good news is that there are existing models for countries that are starting from scratch to build upon. And there’s room for innovation. Established community partnerships and technologies can be leveraged in new ways – for instance, using online learning and video conferencing to help train healthcare workers and build relationships.

We believe pediatric palliative care is the heart of what healthcare should be when a child faces a serious, life-limiting illness, regardless of where they live in the world. Because even when medicine cannot cure, it can always heal and comfort.

articles.title: Menopause can quietly weaken bones – here’s what research reveals about protecting them
articles.author: Priya Bhardwaj, Senior Researcher in Orthopedic Surgery, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: A skeleton hanging on a door or standing in your neighbor’s yard for Halloween looks like a finished structure. But the skeleton inside a living body is constantly changing. Around menopause, those changes can tip toward bone loss, often without pain or another obvious warning.

I am a skeletal biology researcher at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. My work examines how hormonal and metabolic signals influence bone renewal. In my assessment, the quiet nature of bone loss makes menopause an important time to bring skeletal health into the conversation.

Bone loss can start accelerating before the final menstrual period. Natural menopause is confirmed only after 12 consecutive months without a period, when there is no other explanation. Bone loss can therefore accelerate before someone knows that their last period was their final one.
Why bone changes during menopause

Bones are living tissues that continually renew themselves. During this process, called remodeling, cells known as osteoclasts remove old bone while other cells – osteoblasts – build its replacement. Estrogen helps regulate this renewal. As estrogen levels decline around menopause, removal can outpace replacement, contributing to bone loss and osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become more fragile and porous.
Osteoporosis can affect women and men. It becomes more common with age but can also occur in younger people. A person often has no noticeable symptoms until a fracture occurs.

The timing is revealing. An analysis of 862 participants in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation, a long-term U.S. study of women in midlife, tracked changes in bone density in relation to their final menstrual period. On average, loss at the lower spine and near the hip was fastest from about one year before that period through two years afterward. It then slowed rather than stopped.

These findings do not mean that everyone experiences the same amount of bone loss or develops osteoporosis. They show why the menopausal transition itself deserves attention, rather than treating bone loss as a concern only for older women.
Fracture risk and bone loss involve more than age

To assess a person’s risk of breaking a bone, clinicians consider factors such as low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol use and whether a patient’s parent experienced a hip fracture. A bone density scan measures bone mineral density and helps assess fracture risk. It provides useful information alongside medical history and other risk factors.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an independent panel of experts in preventive care, recommends screening for osteoporosis in women age 65 and older. It also recommends screening younger postmenopausal women when their health history and other risk factors indicate a higher chance of a fracture. This does not mean every woman needs a scan as soon as her periods change.

These recommendations address routine screening. People who already have osteoporosis, have broken a bone after a minor fall or have a disease or take medicines that cause bone loss need evaluation tailored to their circumstances.

A U.K. trial illustrates how identifying people at high risk and recommending treatment can help. More than 12,000 women age 70 to 85 received either usual care or screening, followed by treatment recommendations for those at high risk. Over five years, women in the screening group were less likely to break a hip. However, when the researchers considered osteoporosis-related fractures across different parts of the body together, they did not find a statistically significant reduction. The findings support screening linked to treatment in older women, but do not tell us when screening should begin during the menopausal transition.
Movement and nutrition support the skeleton

Bones respond to the forces placed on them. Weight-bearing activities such as walking and stair climbing make bones support the body’s weight. Resistance exercises using weights, bands or body weight create additional forces on bones as muscles pull against them. Balance training, such as tai chi and exercises that practice shifting weight from one foot to the other, can improve stability and help prevent falls. Activity for bone health therefore involves more than one kind of movement.

An Australian trial published in 2018 tested whether supervised heavy resistance exercises and impact movements could improve bone density and physical function in postmenopausal women with low bone mass. After eight months, participants in that program had better results than those following a less intensive home exercise program. The women were carefully screened, and the training was closely supervised.

These improvements are encouraging, but improved bone density is not the same outcome as fewer broken bones: The trial did not establish whether its program reduced fractures. People with osteoporosis, previous fractures or physical limitations may need guidance on appropriate movements and loads. Building muscle strength and balance can support mobility as well as bone health. Choosing suitable exercise depends on a person’s own circumstances.

Nutrition contributes in a different way. Calcium supplies mineral that helps give bones their strength, while vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. Adequate protein also forms part of a balanced diet. Calcium-rich foods include dairy products, fortified alternatives, canned sardines or salmon with edible bones, and vegetables such as bok choy and broccoli.

Calcium or vitamin D supplements may help when a person’s intake is insufficient or they have a deficiency that needs treatment. They do not replace osteoporosis medicines when those are needed. Nutrition and treatment work together.
Treatment depends on the person

Systemic menopausal hormone therapy — treatment that delivers hormones throughout the body — can relieve bothersome hot flashes and night sweats and help prevent bone loss and fractures. Its benefits and risks depend on age, time since menopause, medical history and the treatment used.

For women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset who have no medical reasons to avoid it, the balance of benefits and risks from menopausal hormone therapy is generally favorable for treating troublesome symptoms and preventing bone loss. This does not mean hormone therapy is suitable for everyone. Patients and clinicians should discuss their symptoms, bone health and individual risks, and revisit the decision over time.

Other osteoporosis medicines can slow bone breakdown or stimulate bone formation. Clinicians also consider other medical conditions and medicines that can weaken bones, including hormonal disorders, digestive conditions and long-term glucocorticoid treatment. Menopause may be only part of the explanation.

One example is primary hyperparathyroidism, in which one or more parathyroid glands in the neck produce too much parathyroid hormone. This can raise blood calcium and weaken bones. Identifying it can change the care plan. It illustrates why investigating the cause of bone loss matters, rather than simply attributing it to aging.
Access to care matters, too

Advice about scans and treatment assumes people can obtain them. Looking beyond individual choices shows how access to care can shape the options available. One example comes from a 2025 audit of 22 Asia-Pacific countries and regions. It documented substantial differences in access to osteoporosis care. Bone density scan waits ranged from the same day to nearly a year, and gaps in coverage for medicines limited the affordability of treatment. The regional audit concerns osteoporosis broadly, not only menopause.
In other words, making prevention possible requires both public awareness and health systems that make scans, follow-up care and treatment accessible and affordable.

Menopause offers an opportunity to ask about the skeleton while a person still feels well. The answer may involve a risk assessment, suitable activity, nutritional changes or medical treatment. A bone health conversation can begin long before a fracture starts it.

Priya Bhardwaj is employed by Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. She serves on the Endocrine Society’s Bone and Mineral Special Interest Group steering committee and ASBMR Women in Bone and Mineral SIG Commitee.

articles.title: Climate change is killing hundreds of thousands – a kidney specialist’s concerns
articles.author: Peter Stenvinkel, Professor of Nephrology, Karolinska Institutet
paras: The evidence that climate change threatens human health has never been stronger. Yet a new report suggests that world leaders are giving less attention to its health consequences in international political debate.

The 2026 Lancet Countdown report estimates that heat was associated with 710,000 deaths worldwide in 2023, with around 71% attributable to human-caused climate change. Researchers calculated this by comparing estimated heat-related deaths at the temperatures actually experienced with those expected in a world without human-caused warming. The difference represents the additional deaths associated with climate change.

Heat can cause fatal heatstroke and worsen existing conditions, including heart and kidney disease. The figure is a statistical estimate of the additional deaths caused by warming, rather than a count of individual deaths directly identified as resulting from climate change.

Meanwhile, the proportion of countries whose leaders discussed the relationship between climate change and health during the United Nations General Debate fell from 66% in 2021 to 26% in 2025. The General Debate is the annual gathering at which world leaders address a broad range of international issues.

Europe’s record-breaking heatwaves during the summer of 2026 brought the consequences of rising temperatures into sharp focus. Research examining 854 European cities estimated more than 50,000 heat-related deaths that summer, with around two-thirds attributable to human-caused warming. Using a similar approach, researchers compared the estimated death toll under actual temperatures with the number expected without the additional warming caused by human activity.

Climate change competes with more immediate political concerns, including energy prices, economic pressures and international conflicts. The health benefits of cutting emissions may take time to become visible, while governments face pressure to respond to events unfolding today.

But fewer mentions in UN speeches do not necessarily mean that governments are doing less. The same Lancet Countdown analysis found that 93% of national climate commitments submitted in 2025 mentioned health. Governments may also act through heat-warning systems, cleaner transport or building regulations without repeatedly invoking climate change in international speeches.

The more important question is whether policies deliver measurable protection. Announcing a plan provides little reassurance if vulnerable people remain exposed to dangerous heat or health services lack the resources to respond.
The kidneys reveal a growing health threat

As a kidney physician, I see particular reasons for concern. Chronic kidney disease affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide. The kidneys help filter waste from blood and maintain the body’s balance of water and salts, making them vulnerable when extreme heat disrupts that balance.

Recent research links hot temperatures with increased kidney-related illness. Heat stress and dehydration can contribute to acute kidney injury, particularly among people working in hot conditions and those with existing health problems. Whether repeated heat exposure accelerates chronic kidney disease across the wider population is less certain and remains an important research question.
Air pollution may also affect kidney health. A systematic review found associations between exposure to several common air pollutants and poorer measures of kidney function.
Health benefits that can be felt now
Some climate measures can improve health well before the full benefits of reduced global warming become apparent.

Cleaner energy can reduce harmful air pollution. The Lancet Countdown estimates that declining fossil fuel-related air pollution has helped prevent around 323,000 premature deaths annually across at least 77 countries.

Trees provide shade and cooling in cities, while restored wetlands can help manage flooding and support biodiversity. A review of research on urban trees found consistent cooling benefits, although their effectiveness depends on local climate and how cities are designed.

The healthcare system also has responsibilities. The sector accounts for around 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing waste and unnecessary resource use can contribute to a more sustainable service, provided patient care is protected.
Biodiversity and the library of life

Human health also depends on functioning ecosystems. The international biodiversity science body IPBES has documented how biodiversity loss is connected with threats to water, food and health. Healthy ecosystems are valuable in themselves, and Indigenous peoples and local communities have long contributed knowledge and stewardship essential to their protection.

Nature is also an extraordinary library of biological solutions developed through evolution. Many medicines have come from natural products or compounds inspired by them. Scientists are now exploring how artificial intelligence can help identify promising compounds from biological data, potentially speeding up early stages of drug discovery. These possibilities are exciting, but translating a promising compound into a safe and effective treatment requires extensive research.

Protecting biodiversity is therefore relevant to both present health and future scientific discoveries. AI may help researchers understand some of nature’s complexity, but it cannot restore an extinct species or replace the ecological knowledge held by communities.

The political challenge is to connect the evidence of harm from climate change with practical decisions that protect people. Climate change is already affecting health, and the benefits to human health of protecting the environment are not confined to some distant future.
Destroying the natural systems that sustain health while scientists are still learning how they work would be a costly mistake.
Peter Stenvinkel receives funding from CIMED, Heart and Lung-Foundation, ALF and Westman Foundation.

articles.title: Sunscreen myths explained: the truth about beef tallow, cancer and vitamin D
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Some people are so worried about sunscreen that they’re swapping factor 50 for beef tallow. Yes, the fat traditionally used to make roast potatoes is now being promoted online as something you can spread on your skin before going into the sun.

Coconut oil and olive oil have their supporters, too. Meanwhile, other social media creators warn that conventional sunscreens contain dangerous chemicals, interfere with our hormones or prevent us from making vitamin D. Some even claim sunscreen causes cancer.
But how much of this is backed by science? And what happens to your skin when you swap a tested sunscreen for something from the kitchen cupboard?

In the latest episode of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast about unusual health and wellness trends, I investigate the anti-sunscreen movement with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

There’s a revealing twist to the social media story. A 2026 study examining 971 popular sunscreen-related TikToks found that almost 87% promoted sunscreen use. Only 6% included health-related criticism. Yet videos devoted to criticism attracted substantially more likes, shares and comments than those focused solely on promotion.
Can sunscreen really be harmful?
Our guest is Charareh Pourzand, a professor of pharmaceutical biology at the University of Bath, who has spent more than 30 years investigating how sunlight affects skin.

She helps us unpick concerns about sunscreen ingredients. Some UV filters can be absorbed into the bloodstream, and certain ingredients have shown hormonal activity in laboratory studies. But finding a substance in the body, or an effect in a laboratory, doesn’t establish that normal sunscreen use causes harm.

Regulators continue to review the evidence. The UK has recently restricted one UV filter in sunscreen, known as 4-MBC, after a safety assessment. That scrutiny is important, as is the extensive evidence that ultraviolet radiation damages skin and increases skin cancer risk.

Then there’s vitamin D. Sunscreen limits UVB radiation (a specific type of ultraviolet light), which the skin uses to make the vitamin. But that doesn’t justify deliberately exposing yourself to harmful ultraviolet light when vitamin D can also come from food or supplements.
Why a homemade sunscreen is a gamble

Pourzand explains why mixing oils or beef tallow into a homemade sunscreen is risky. Even if an ingredient absorbs some UV radiation, you won’t know how reliably the mixture protects your skin without proper formulation and testing.
We also discuss sunbeds, the myth of a protective “base tan”, and Pourzand’s research into how sunlight can release iron inside skin cells, amplifying damage.

And Dan explains why the most expensive sunscreen isn’t necessarily the best purchase. What counts is choosing tested protection against both UVA and UVB radiation, applying enough and reapplying when needed. We also consider whether you really need SPF (sun protection factor) 50 for a short trip outdoors on a British winter day.
Listen to the episode before your next attempt to turn the kitchen cupboard into a skincare counter.
Have you spotted a bizarre health trend you’d like us to investigate? Email strangehealth@theconversation.com. The stranger the question, the better.

articles.title: Why people trust weight-loss drug advice on social media, even when it may be misleading
articles.author: Andy Levy, Reader in Psychology, Edge Hill University
paras: Imagine scrolling through social media and seeing dramatic weight-loss results from people taking Mounjaro, Wegovy or Ozempic. They share photographs, discuss side effects and recommend ways to get the best results.

These personal stories can feel convincing, especially when they come from people with similar experiences. For someone struggling with their weight, advice from a supportive online community may seem more relatable than information from a medical professional.

A 2026 UK study involving 684 adults, including 544 current or former users of weight-loss medications, found that 48% of participants used social media as a source of information about the drugs. Healthcare professionals were consulted less frequently.

Although the survey cannot tell us how widespread this behaviour is across the UK, it raises an interesting question: why might people trust advice from strangers online, even when medical professionals can offer more reliable information?
Psychology offers some clues.
Why personal stories carry so much weight

People are often more receptive to advice from those they see as members of their own group. Psychologists call this social identity: the sense of identity we gain from belonging to groups with shared experiences, interests or goals.

When someone identifies strongly with a group, they may pay particular attention to what other members say and do. Advice from people who share their experiences can feel more relevant and trustworthy, even when those people have no medical expertise.
For someone who has experienced judgement about their weight, finding people who understand their difficulties can be especially valuable.

In research I co-authored, we explored how a shared sense of identity could be encouraged in a group-based exercise rehabilitation programme for people with chronic lung disease. Although we did not test whether this improved outcomes, the work illustrated how a sense of belonging might encourage mutual support.
Similar psychological processes may help explain the appeal of online weight-loss communities.

The difficulty arises when trust in someone with shared experiences extends to their medical advice. A person may genuinely have benefited from a medication without understanding its risks or whether their experience is typical.
How online groups shape what people believe
Online communities can provide encouragement and practical support, but they can also influence which experiences receive attention and which opinions become widely accepted.

A 2021 study involving interviews with 32 people in a professionally supervised online weight-management programme in China found that peer support encouraged motivation and a sense of belonging. However, comparisons with other members could also reinforce unhelpful group expectations.
Similar pressures may arise in online communities discussing weight-loss medication.

For example, someone who repeatedly sees dramatic success stories may begin to expect the same results from their own treatment. If a particular medication is widely praised, questioning its effectiveness or discussing negative experiences might feel uncomfortable.
These influences do not affect everyone in the same way, but they help explain how advice can become accepted within a group, even when there is limited medical evidence to support it.
And the information circulating online is not always reliable.
An October 2026 study examined 194 popular TikTok and YouTube Shorts videos about weight-loss medications, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, the active ingredients in Wegovy and Mounjaro.

Only 24% of all views of the assessed videos were for content researchers judged to be medically accurate. Some videos contained incorrect medical information, while others provided too little clinical information to assess their accuracy.
The researchers examined a selected group of popular videos, so their findings cannot be generalised to everything shared about weight-loss drugs online.
Nevertheless, the findings illustrate how a video can attract considerable attention without providing the information someone needs to make a safe medical decision.
The risks of unregulated weight-loss drugs

The consequences can become more serious when online recommendations move beyond sharing experiences of prescribed medicines to encouraging people to obtain drugs that have not been approved for medical use.
One example is “Reta”, the nickname for retatrutide, an experimental weight-loss medication being developed by pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly.
Retatrutide has produced substantial weight loss in clinical trials, but it has not been authorised for medical use in the UK. Its benefits and risks are still being assessed.
Despite this, products marketed as “Reta” have been supplied through unregulated channels.
In October 2026, the UK medicines regulator seized more than 12,000 counterfeit weight-loss injection pens labelled as retatrutide or tirzepatide from a Birmingham industrial unit.
Products supplied through these channels may contain incorrect ingredients, unreliable doses or harmful contaminants.

There is an important distinction between these products and regulated prescription medicines. Mounjaro and Wegovy are authorised for weight management in the UK when prescribed appropriately. Ozempic contains semaglutide, the same active ingredient as Wegovy, but is licensed for treating type 2 diabetes.
Even approved medicines can cause side effects and require appropriate medical assessment.
A personal recommendation, however convincing, cannot establish whether an unregulated product is genuine or safe.
Making better-informed decisions

Online weight-loss communities can provide valuable emotional support, particularly for people who feel isolated or judged. The challenge is recognising when shared experiences begin to influence decisions that require medical expertise.

Before following advice about weight-loss medication, consider whether the person recommending it is promoting a product or receiving payment. Be particularly wary of dramatic promises, suggestions to change prescribed doses without medical advice or offers to supply medication outside regulated pharmacies.

It is also worth considering whether an online community welcomes discussion of side effects and disappointing experiences, or predominantly celebrates positive results. Groups that allow people to question claims may provide a more balanced picture.

Anyone considering weight-loss medication should seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional. The UK medicines regulator advises obtaining these medicines only with a valid prescription from a registered pharmacy.
Understanding how group identity influences trust can help people recognise the value of online support while being more critical of the medical advice they encounter.
Shared experiences can offer reassurance and encouragement, but decisions about medication should be informed by reliable evidence and individual medical advice.

articles.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
articles.author: Sarah Chellappa, Associate Professor, Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, University of Southampton
paras: Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role.
Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion.

Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut.
When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges.

Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning.
These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing.
In a 2024 laboratory study, my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities.
We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour.

We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines.
Circadian disruption has also been linked to depression and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood.

The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another.
What happens when our clocks fall out of sync
Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness.
This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment.
In a 2020 study, we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience.

Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep.

We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers.
These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences.
Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as social jetlag. This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off.
Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time.

My research on light sensitivity has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects.
Could changing meal times help?
Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs.
In a 2022 study, my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood.
Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime.
Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements.
We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime.

These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression.
How to support your body clock
Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned.

Get morning daylight. Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people.

Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The NHS recommends avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime.

Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A systematic review associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression.

Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A review of studies found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did.
Protecting sleep and mental health

Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions.

Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health.

articles.title: When a bull falls for a donkey: what an unlikely relationship reveals about animal sexuality
articles.author: Jo Setchell, Professor of Anthropology, Durham University
paras: On an Ethiopian plateau, a bull called Achille formed an unusual relationship with a male donkey named Patroclo. They were observed spending time together, licking and rubbing against one another, and repeatedly having penetrative sex.

The animals’ names nod to Achilles and Patroclus, the Greek mythological figures whose bond has been debated for thousands of years: devoted friends – or lovers? A new study in the journal Current Biology asks something similar about Achille and Patroclo: why would two males of different species repeatedly choose each other as sexual partners when females of their own species are available?
Perhaps the more interesting question is why we find their relationship so surprising.
The researchers first noticed Achille and Patroclo while studying gelada monkeys in Ethiopia. Intrigued, they began observing the pair more closely.

They recorded 51 mounting attempts, 34 of which involved penetration. Patroclo took an active role, presenting his hindquarters to Achille and initiating contact. Unlike another male donkey that Achille approached, Patroclo did not show obvious signs of trying to avoid him.
The donkey and bull often showed affection towards each other immediately after mounting. This suggests that sex may help strengthen their bond.

The researchers observed the pair in detail for just four days, so they cannot say how long the relationship lasted. Even so, the findings are unusual because the two animals are both male and belong to different species.

Same-sex sexual behaviour has been reported in more than 1,500 animal species. A 2023 study documented it in 261 mammalian species and found that it was particularly associated with social species, suggesting a possible role in maintaining relationships and managing conflict.

As a primatologist, I am not surprised by these findings. Bonobos, for example, are famous for their frequent sexual interactions, which occur in many combinations of partners. Female–female genital rubbing, for instance, is associated with affiliation and social bonding. Sexual interactions can also help manage social tensions.

Same-sex sexual behaviour takes many forms. Male bottlenose dolphins mount one another and rub genitals in groups that cooperate to gain access to females, while female Japanese macaques form temporary sexual partnerships involving repeated mounting. Same-sex sexual behaviour may play a part in establishing status, settling disputes, forming friendships or sexual enjoyment.

Sexual behaviour between different species is rarer, but it is not unheard of. Both male and female Japanese macaques, for example, mount sika deer. Unlike the apparently reciprocal relationship between Achille and Patroclo, these encounters do not necessarily involve mutual sexual interest.
What makes Achille and Patroclo particularly interesting is that they combine sexual activity with apparent affection and a preference for each other.

Evolutionary biologists have traditionally approached same-sex sexual behaviour as a puzzle. If natural selection favours traits that contribute to reproductive success, why should animals spend time and energy engaging in sexual behaviour that cannot directly produce offspring?

Suggested explanations include mistaken identity, a lack of opposite-sex partners, or indiscriminate sexual behaviour with whichever individuals happen to be nearby. But all these explanations begin with an assumption that sexual behaviour between males and females is the default, and same-sex behaviour represents a departure from it.

In a provocative 2019 paper, a team of researchers challenged this assumption. They proposed that the ancestors of sexually reproducing animals may have been relatively indiscriminate about the sex of their sexual partners. Rather than assuming that different-sex sexual behaviour came first, they suggested that the ability to distinguish between potential partners, and preferentially direct sexual behaviour towards the opposite sex, may have evolved later.
Taking a queer perspective
This is a brilliant example of how queer perspectives can enrich evolutionary biology.

Queer approaches encourage scientists to examine how human assumptions about sex, gender and sexuality influence the questions we ask, the categories we use and the explanations we consider plausible. They do not require us to assign human sexual identities to animals.

Observing same-sex sexual behaviour does not tell us that an animal is gay or establish a fixed sexual orientation. Instead, queer approaches encourage us to take the diversity of animal sexual behaviour seriously, without assuming what is normal or what needs explaining.

The authors of the new study suggest that Achille and Patroclo’s sexual interactions may help maintain their social relationship. They also discuss the possible reproductive costs of spending time and energy on sexual activity that cannot result in offspring.
But this framing raises another question. Why should we assume that sexual behaviour must contribute directly to reproduction to have evolutionary significance?

Social relationships can influence survival, access to resources and future reproductive opportunities. Sexual behaviour that strengthens those relationships may therefore have adaptive benefits, even when it cannot directly produce offspring. Equally, sexual behaviour may arise from evolved mechanisms without every individual encounter necessarily providing an animal’s reproductive success.

Achille and Patroclo cannot tell us why they choose one another. This short study can’t tell us what evolutionary purpose, if any, their relationship serves. But it does remind us that animal behaviour can be more diverse than our theories suggest.

Perhaps the most important lesson is not that a bull and a donkey have formed an unusual sexual relationship. It is that understanding such relationships requires us to question our assumptions about what sex is, what it does, and what counts as natural.

articles.title: The surprising science of what pain is and why it hurts
articles.author: Dave Newell, Professor of Integrated Musculoskeletal Care and Head of the Centre of Pain and Active Inference Research, Health Sciences University
paras: When you step into an ice-cold lake, it would be nice if your body warned you about possible harm with a polite message: “Your feet may be at risk. Would you kindly consider stepping out?”

Instead, your feet hurt. A lot. Your attention narrows and getting out becomes an urgent priority. Friends’ promises of fun suddenly matter much less. Why does information about possible bodily harm feel so unpleasant? Why can’t we register the danger as calmly as we take in the lakeside trees?
Part of the answer begins with another question: what is perception for?

Perception helps living things navigate the world: finding food, avoiding danger and maintaining a healthy body. All of this helps us survive. But how does a nervous system figure out what is happening and what to do next?

We seem to experience the world directly: the lake, the trees, our friends wondering why we’re making such a hasty exit. But the brain receives neither light nor sound directly. Instead, information from your eyes, ears, skin and internal organs reaches it through signals that include brief electrical impulses called “action potentials”. These signals carry no labels explaining what they mean. Yet you experience trees, voices and freezing feet.

Predictive theories of perception offer a counterintuitive explanation. They propose that your nervous system uses experience to predict, or make educated guesses about, what incoming sensory information means. Sensory signals are then used to check those predictions and revise them when they do not fit.

In this account, experience emerges from an ongoing exchange between predictions and sensory information. The world does not simply pour in through our senses. The nervous system helps construct our experience while continually checking it against signals from the world and body.

This educated guessing is called inference: drawing conclusions from incomplete information. Through experience, the nervous system learns patterns, sometimes called models, that help it anticipate what sensations might come next. You do not consult these patterns consciously. They are at work as you read, recognise a voice or feel painfully cold feet.

We usually assume that something acts on our senses first, followed by a sensation: the icy lake bathes your skin and then your feet feel cold and hurt. However, predictive accounts of pain suggest that unconscious interpretation helps shape the feeling itself. You do not first experience electrical signals and then give them meaning. What you feel may depend partly on how your nervous system interprets those signals at that moment.

There is evidence that expectations influence pain. In one experiment involving ten volunteers, researchers applied painful heat to their legs. When participants expected less intense heat than they actually received, they rated the same heat about 28% less painful. Brain scans also showed reduced activity in regions involved in processing pain. This demonstrates an effect of expectation, although it does not establish that predictive processing fully explains pain.
These predictions are not a conscious decision about whether something should hurt. Both information from the body and learned expectations matter; neither alone determines the experience.

A related framework, called “active inference”, links perception with action: what we feel influences how we act, and how we act changes what we experience. Living things do not just update predictions. They act to change what happens next, including the next set of information their senses receive.

In the lake, pain makes a possible threat feel urgent and prompts protective action. Getting out changes the signals reaching your nervous system. Feeling cold, feeling pain and wanting to escape are connected parts of a response aimed at protecting your body.

Sensory nerves also detect potentially damaging conditions, such as extreme cold. This process is called nociception. It provides important information, but it is not identical to pain, the unpleasant experience itself. The nervous system also draws on previous experience, expectations and circumstances when interpreting that information.
This helps explain why the intensity of pain does not necessarily correspond to the extent of tissue damage. Pain can persist without continuing injury.

Consider persistent back pain. Someone who has repeatedly felt pain when bending may anticipate it and move cautiously. Avoiding bending may bring relief, but also limit opportunities to learn whether movement has become safer or more manageable. Research links fear of movement with persistent back pain, although the evidence is uncertain.

One of us (Michael Thacker) and colleagues have proposed that active inference could help explain how past experiences shape feelings and actions. This is only one possible contributor to persistent pain, which can also involve ongoing tissue injury or damage to nerves. It does not imply that people consciously think themselves into pain.

So why does pain hurt? Active inference suggests that unpleasantness helps make a possible threat important enough to demand protection. But protection is not always useful. Pain can persist without continuing damage, and actions intended to protect us can sometimes become disabling. The theory suggests what unpleasantness might achieve, although it has not fully explained how the feeling itself arises.

Predictive theories still need further testing, particularly to establish whether they improve care. Their hopeful suggestion is that pain might be better understood through the relationship between the body, experience, action and circumstances, without ever doubting that the suffering of people with persistent pain is real.

articles.title: Parents, let your kids eat as much candy as they want – less restriction could help reduce the urge to overeat
articles.author: Bryn Beeder, Assistant Clinical Lecturer in Kinesiology, Nutrition, and Health, Miami University
paras: Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats. But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume.

As a registered dietitian and mom of three, I understand the stress that comes with wanting to encourage healthy food choices without removing all the fun of childhood traditions. I also believe the answer to this dilemma may be simpler than the familiar back and forth of “Just one more piece of candy!” and “Haven’t you had enough already?”

Research suggests that by managing the candy inventory less and encouraging more autonomy around sweets, parents can help their kids practice tapping into their hunger and fullness cues, promoting a healthier relationship with food over time.

There is no question that some foods have greater nutritional value than others. A piece of cake – carrot cake included – will never provide the vitamins and minerals of a large garden salad. As a result, people often categorize different foods as “good” or “bad.”

The tendency to place food in two polarizing buckets can affect everything from what foods you purchase at the grocery store to the language you use to describe food. The problem is, “good” and “bad” are moral concepts. When morality is consistently applied to food, a person’s relationship to food can become complicated. Instead of viewing food as fueling, it can become a measuring stick for whether your food choices are something to feel proud of or guilty about.

When a person’s inner monologue about food is preoccupied with whether it is good or bad for their health or diet plan, food choices can become less about enjoyment and more about their willpower to make the “right” decision at the grocery store and at mealtimes. Any guilt or shame that comes from this evaluation can spill over into what foods are served freely at home and which are restricted.
Restriction leads to overeating

The idea of food restriction often sounds punishing. For parents and others who take care of children, food restriction often may simply be an attempt to limit sugary foods and introduce more fruits and vegetables.

But for kids, restricting certain foods may lead them to become preoccupied with those foods. They may be nagged by the knowledge that the foods adults often call “bad” are also the ones that are really delicious. What started as a simple candy rule can continue to influence a child’s relationship to food and eating long after the treats are gone.

Parents often approach food restriction in two different ways. In overt food restriction, kids are aware that their parents or guardians are limiting access to specific foods because they can see it or are told specific foods are off limits. In practice, this might mean the kids know candy is in the house but stored out of reach in the kitchen cupboards. Parents or caregivers who practice covert food restriction, on the other hand, may choose to not buy bags of candy at all in order to encourage more balanced food choices.

Research suggests that overt restriction can unintentionally increase kids’ interest in those restricted food items. That preoccupation may mean the child has a more difficult time listening to their fullness cues when presented with those foods. If bags of candy are usually stored out of reach, it may be tempting to eat more than just a few pieces when access is finally granted – and they may completely ignore any signs that their body is full.

Incorporating neutral language about food at mealtimes and encouraging kids to eat according to their own hunger and fullness cues can help them build trust in their bodies and improve family connection at the table. Taking the pressure off finishing all the food on the plate can instead place emphasis on savoring the sensory experience of each bite.

Eating according to internal cues is one part of intuitive eating, which aims to increase a person’s trust in their own body to signal when to start eating and when to stop. Kids can also benefit from this same framework, with some age-appropriate modifications.

The Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding provides a simple, research-based approach to feeding kids in a way that avoids power struggles between kids and caretakers at the table. Developed by the Ellyn Satter Institute, a nonprofit focused on improving people’s relationship to food, the goal of the framework is to introduce intuitive eating in a kid-friendly way. When providing food through this approach, parents decide when and what food is served, while kids are in charge of deciding what and how much they eat from their plates. The emphasis is on helping kids eat according to their internal cues without pressuring them to eat specific foods.

Candy can be a part of the menu rotation in this feeding framework. Repeatedly exposing kids to a variety of foods, including sugary treats outside of special holidays or events, means no food becomes emphasized for being better or worse than another food – it is all simply food.

This approach can shift the conversation to how different foods affect their bodies in different ways: Some food – like candy – makes them run super fast, some foods grow their muscles, while other foods keep their eyes strong.
Building healthier relationships with food

Regularly using neutral language to describe food and exposing kids to a variety of foods helps reduce the power that sugary treats have over their appetites. This doesn’t mean birthday cake, doughnuts and candy will no longer taste delicious. It simply means children can rest assured they will see their favorite treats again without the added urge to overconsume them.
If you’re interested in exploring how intuitive eating principles could change your child’s or your own relationship with food, here are a few practices you can try at home:

Involve children in menu planning and grocery shopping. Let your kids pick a treat to add to a few meals each week, and serve the treat with the rest of the food on the menu for that day. Presenting all food items at the same time on the plate – versus saving a dessert or treat for after the meal – visually reminds everyone that food does not have to be earned. Rather, each food nourishes their bodies in different ways.

Avoid commenting on what your kids eat. It can be tempting to praise a child when they choose to take a bite of the broccoli you’ve been encouraging for weeks. Praising kids for eating certain foods versus others can create a food hierarchy, leading them to think about food as a way to earn a reward instead of fueling their body.

Challenge your own relationship with food. Do you eat when you are hungry and stop when you are full? Do you restrict your own food cravings as a punishment, or do you struggle to control yourself when eating a treat you love? Kids are always watching, and your own food behaviors often speak louder than words.

Consider letting your kids indulge for a day. In my own family, I don’t limit how much candy my three kids eat on Halloween night. I won’t lie – they usually eat quite a bit. When they mention a stomachache afterward, we talk about how eating a lot of candy can make their bodies feel – without adding judgment. Their interest typically fades over the next few days while we continue to offer a piece of two with meals. Eventually the extras become props for elaborate trick-or-treat pretend play.
One day or evening of holiday eating does not define their health, but fun memories with friends and families can last a lifetime. So let them eat … candy!

articles.title: Florida Department of Health considers dropping 4 school vaccine requirements – here’s what that could mean for kids
articles.author: Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago
paras: The Florida Department of Health held a hearing in October 2026 on a proposal to remove four vaccine requirements for entry into school and childcare: Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib, chickenpox, pneumococcal and hepatitis B.

These vaccines entered use in the U.S. at different times from the early 1980s through 2000. Prior to that, there were millions of chickenpox cases and thousands of serious bacterial infections and preventable deaths among American children each year. Vaccination has dramatically reduced the toll of these diseases.

Many parents today grew up during the transition to widespread vaccination for these diseases and may never have witnessed the severe complications these vaccines help prevent. I’m an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication, and I worry that perhaps the luxury of forgetting about these diseases could end up giving rise to a generation of children who aren’t vaccinated against them.
What Florida would be choosing

School vaccination requirements help communities establish herd immunity, which is when enough people are vaccinated to prevent a disease from easily spreading. When vaccination rates fall, infections can spread among susceptible children throughout the community, placing those who are too young to be fully vaccinated, as well as those who cannot develop adequate protection due to medical conditions, at greater risk.

Florida’s proposal would not eliminate these four vaccines, nor would ending a mandate mean that every family would stop using them. However, it would weaken one of the policies designed to maintain high vaccination coverage. If fewer children are vaccinated as a result, the risks will extend beyond the families making that choice.
The consequences could be devastating.
Hib: The bacterium that can cause meningitis

Before Hib vaccines became widely used in the late 1980s, pediatricians sometimes faced a terrifying emergency: an infant with fever, lethargy and a stiff neck. Testing of cerebrospinal fluid would reveal bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib, an infection that could kill a child or leave lasting neurological damage.
Today, many doctors have never even seen a single case. The bacterium has not disappeared, but widespread vaccination has made serious Hib disease in young children far less common.

Before the vaccine, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis. In the early 1980s, there were 20,000 invasive Hib infections among American children under 5 years old, 12,000 of which were meningitis. Between 3% and 6% of those children died, and between 15% and 30% of the survivors were left deaf or with brain damage.
Hib infection did not manifest in dramatic outbreaks. Healthy young children carried it silently, and some, unpredictably, became seriously ill.

After the introduction of conjugate vaccines for Hib in the late 1980s, cases among young children declined by 99%. In 2023, the United States reported only 13 cases in children under 5. In 2026, that number is up to 28.
Chickenpox: The ‘harmless’ rite of passage

By the early 1990s, there were more than 4 million cases of chickenpox annually in the United States. Of those infected, 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized, and 100 to 150 died. More than 90% of cases and about 70% of hospitalizations occurred in children, as did roughly half of the deaths.
But even those who had manageable cases of childhood chickenpox are at risk for shingles later in life, which can lead to painful and sometimes permanent health complications.

Children are contagious before the rash appears, and each case has an incubation period of up to three weeks. A single infection could spread through a school or daycare in waves for a month or more. Since vaccination began in 1995, deaths from chickenpox in people under 20 years old have been virtually eliminated.
Pneumococcus: Serious infections
Pneumococcal bacteria can live harmlessly in a child’s upper respiratory tract – that is, the nose – but if it moves into the blood or organs, it can cause serious damage.

Before the introduction of the childhood vaccine in 2000, pneumococcal disease caused about 17,000 invasive infections annually in American children under 5 years old, including about 700 cases of meningitis and 200 deaths. On top of that, pneumococcal disease caused approximately 5 million ear infections.
Hepatitis B: The silent threat

Hepatitis B can spread from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth and through contact with infected blood. People with chronic hepatitis B may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected, allowing the virus to spread unknowingly within families and communities. Infected infants and young children also are often asymptomatic.

Yet the consequences can be serious. Infants who become infected with hepatitis B have about a 90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B, which over time can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The risk of chronic infection falls sharply with age, making prevention of infection early in life particularly important.
Before the hepatitis B vaccine became available in the U.S. in 1982, an estimated 20,000 American children were infected each year.

In 1991, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended universal infant hepatitis B vaccination as part of a comprehensive strategy to prevent transmission. The CDC estimates that perinatal hepatitis B infections in the United States declined by 75% between 1987 and 2000.

Florida’s historical records for these diseases are incomplete. For example, chickenpox was not a disease tracked by the Florida Department of Health until late 2006. That makes it difficult to reconstruct the state’s prevaccine impact of these diseases from surveillance records alone.

But Florida doesn’t have to imagine what happens when vaccination is neglected: Measles has resurfaced in the state this year. It had previously been eliminated nationally in 2000, meaning sustained endemic transmission had been interrupted. The disease has never been eradicated globally, and imported infections can trigger outbreaks when they reach undervaccinated communities.

An outbreak at Ave Maria University outside of Naples infected at least 62 people, and the state reported 162 cases as of Oct. 17, 2026. This is the most recent available data at the time of this article’s publication.

The proposal to stop requiring vaccines for hepatitis B, chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal comes as only 88.9% of Florida kindergartners received the measles, mumps, rubella – or MMR – vaccine during the 2025-26 school year. This is below both the U.S. national average of 92.4% and the recommended threshold of 95% to create herd immunity.

Unfortunately, it’s been difficult to know current measles rates in Florida. In May 2026, the Florida Department of Health removed county-level disease data from its website. The data has since been replaced, but there is currently no measles dashboard to track cases in the state. The department’s 2026 counts have often been delayed, and public tracking systems disagree on the statewide total.

An entire generation of parents has been spared the experience of seeing a child with Hib meningitis, or young adults with liver problems from chronic hepatitis B. Nor have they had to deal with finding alternate childcare for a month because a chickenpox outbreak has shut down their child’s preschool. These are achievements of vaccination – and a reminder of what can be forgotten when prevention works.

articles.title: Not all antihistamines are the same – and some may affect your brain more than you think
articles.author: Dipa Kamdar, Associate Professor in Pharmacy Practice, Kingston University
paras: Millions of people take antihistamines for allergies, but some of these medicines can make you sleepy, slow your reactions and affect your concentration. Others are much less likely to have these effects. Knowing the difference can help you choose an allergy treatment that won’t interfere with your day.

Antihistamines work by blocking histamine, a chemical released by the immune system during an allergic reaction. Histamine causes many common allergy symptoms, including itching, sneezing, watery eyes and a runny nose.

The first antihistamines were developed in the 1940s. Medicines such as chlorphenamine, diphenhydramine and promethazine are known as first-generation antihistamines, and they are still widely available in allergy medicines, cold remedies and sleep aids.

In the 1980s and 1990s, newer antihistamines such as loratadine, cetirizine and fexofenadine were introduced. Known as second-generation antihistamines, they were designed to cause fewer side-effects, especially drowsiness.

The reason some antihistamines cause drowsiness while others do not comes down to what happens in the brain. Older antihistamines can easily cross the blood-brain barrier, which helps control what enters the brain from the bloodstream. There, they block histamine receptors that help keep you alert and awake.

Brain imaging studies show that older antihistamines block more histamine receptors in the brain than newer ones. This is linked to a greater risk of sleepiness, slower reaction times and difficulty concentrating.

Newer antihistamines generally have less effect on the brain, although there are differences between medicines. One study found that fexofenadine occupied around 2% of histamine receptors in the brain, compared with 24% for cetirizine (a second-generation drug) and 50 to 60% for chlorpheniramine. This helps explain why some “non-drowsy” antihistamines may still cause sleepiness in certain people.

Researchers increasingly recognise that antihistamines do not fall neatly into two groups: those that cause sleepiness and those that do not. Instead, they are better viewed as existing on a spectrum.

Some older antihistamines have a strong effect on alertness; some newer medicines have a mild effect and others have very little effect on the brain at all. This is why two medicines that treat the same allergy symptoms can leave you feeling quite different.
Some people find the sedative effects useful. Diphenhydramine, for example, is sold in several over-the-counter sleep aids. But feeling sleepy is not always harmless.

Antihistamines can affect attention, memory, coordination and reaction times. This can make activities such as driving or operating machinery less safe. You may not realise how much you are affected: even if you feel only slightly tired, your reactions may be slower and your concentration poorer.

For people who need regular allergy treatment, newer antihistamines are generally recommended because they are less likely to cause sleepiness. Some second-generation antihistamines, particularly cetirizine, can still cause drowsiness in some people, though the effect is usually less pronounced than with older medicines.
Sleepiness is not the only concern with older antihistamines. Many also affect another chemical messenger in the body, giving them what are known as anticholinergic effects.

As well as blocking histamine, these medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger that helps the brain control memory, learning and attention. It also plays a role in other functions throughout the body.

Newer antihistamines act more specifically on histamine receptors involved in allergic symptoms and have weaker acetylcholine effects. They are also less likely to enter the brain. As a result, they generally cause fewer unwanted effects than older antihistamines.

In the short term, medicines with anticholinergic effects can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness and confusion. These effects can be more serious in older people and may raise the risk of falls resulting in an increasing likelihood of hospital stays and losing the ability to live independently.

Scientists have also explored whether medicines with anticholinergic effects, including first-generation antihistamines, could affect brain health. The research hasn’t proved that these medicines directly caused dementia. But the findings have strengthened advice to avoid unnecessary use of anticholinergic medicines, especially among older people.
Why are older antihistamines still available?

Despite these concerns, older antihistamines remain widely available. Many people buy the same medicines they have used for years. Others appreciate the sedative effects, particularly when symptoms such as itching or hay fever interfere with sleep.

Older antihistamines can still be useful for treating allergies. But people who drive, who need to concentrate on studying or who take several other medicines may be better off with an option that is less likely to cause sleepiness.

Before choosing an allergy tablet, check which antihistamine it contains. Medicines that treat the same symptoms can have very different effects on how alert you feel, so the right choice can make a difference to your day.
