articles.title: Can creatine help your mental health? Here’s what the latest evidence says
articles.author: Zudin Puthucheary, Professor of Intensive Care Medicine, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Once a supplement favoured mainly by fitness fanatics, creatine has quickly become one of the most widely used dietary add-ons in the world.

While its advantages for strength and athletic performance are supported by evidence, it’s increasingly being recommended for its mental health effects. In fact, a recent review has even suggested the supplement may have benefits as a treatment for depression.

There are many reasons why creatine appears to be beneficial for our brains and mental health. But before you start taking the supplement for your wellbeing, it’s important to understand the nuance of what the research has found so far.
Creatine is a compound that our bodies naturally make. It’s also found in meat (both white and red) and some fish (including salmon, tuna, cod and herring).

Creatine acts as a source of energy in the body. It primarily helps deliver energy to our muscles when we’re active. Most of our creatine is stored in our muscles, with small amounts also stored in the brain.

The brain is one of the most energy-hungry organs in the body. Although it only accounts for 2% of our total body weight, it uses 20% of the body’s energy – especially during complex thinking and tasks.

When energy is low in the brain, it can affect the important chemicals that control mood. Low brain energy is also thought to contribute to different types of mental health issues, including depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Research also found that people who are depressed can have low levels of creatine in the front of their brains, a key area associated with mood.
This is why it has been suggested that creatine may be useful for treating mental health conditions, including depression.
Forty years ago, scientists found a relationship between having suicidal thoughts and low creatine levels.
Since then, numerous studies have investigated whether there’s a link between creatine levels and mental health.
Large studies have found that people who consume more creatine have lower rates of depression.

Research has also found that teenagers with treatment-resistant depression who took creatine supplements alongside their usual medication found their mood improved. The same was true in people with bipolar disorder, who reported that using a creatine supplement alongside their normal medication improved symptoms.

To get a better overview of what benefit creatine has on mental health, a recent systematic review was conducted. They looked at five trials and 238 patients. Two of the trials showed a benefit; three did not.

However, it’s important to note that each of these trials was small, and they all tested different questions. For instance, some tested creatine by itself, some tested whether taking creatine alongside antidepressants had an effect, and others tested whether taking creatine alongside psychotherapy had benefits.
The doses of creatine and the amount of time people took the supplement also varied significantly. This makes it hard to draw a firm conclusion, so better trials are needed.
Researchers are also investigating whether creatine can benefit other areas of cognitive health – particularly those related to memory.
Our brain’s ability to process and use information is highly energy dependent. If that energy supply is disrupted, it can affect how we process and remember information.

For instance, sleep deprivation is known to affect many aspects of cognitive function – including attention and memory processing. Research points to a lack of brain energy as a potential explanation.
Studies scanning human brains have found that in people who are sleep deprived, the brain uses more creatine. This can affect how much available creatine is stored in the body.
Research has also found that topping up creatine stores after a bad night’s sleep could counteract the effects of sleep deprivation on the brain.

A study of 15 healthy people explored the effect of taking a single, high dose of creatine (around 25g) on sleep deprivation and cognitive function. Brain scans of the participants showed that sleep deprivation had decreased brain creatine stores. But when they took the creatine, the scans showed it was used by the brain.
The participants who took the creatine also saw improvements on short-term memory tasks, reaction speed and information processing compared to the group who did not receive creatine.

This small study is not enough proof to recommend creatine for sleep deprivation. But considering that sleep deprivation is also linked to increased risk of anxiety and depression, this could be a useful, short-term strategy for looking after cognitive health.
Because brain energy affects so many things, there’s also interest in what effects it might have on other brain diseases.
Impaired brain energy is considered an important factor in the progression of Alzheimer’s disease. Many parts of the brain affected by Alzheimer’s also appear to have low creatine levels.

Only one very small study has investigated this link. Although the study found creatine had encouraging effects on fluid intelligence (ability to think abstractly and reason quickly), reading and working memory in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, more research is needed before it can be recommended as a treatment.
It’s important to note that all of the studies that have explored creatine’s benefits for mental health or cognitive health have been quite small – so there’s no conclusive scientific evidence yet.

We also don’t know the right dose or how long to take it for. It may be that a person needs to take a higher creatine dose and for a longer period than they would if they were just taking it for fitness. This is because creatine doesn’t transport easily into the brain. It will be important to understand which dose is right for the brain, and whether that dosage is still safe.
For now, the best thing to do is to ensure you eat enough creatine as part of a balanced diet.
Zudin Puthucheary is affiliated with the Intensive Care Society and the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death.

articles.title: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
articles.author: Lindsey Murtagh, Distinguished Senior Fellow in Health Law, Brown University
paras: Imagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network.
Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible.

A law called the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead.

As a health policy researcher and a former federal employee who helped draft the rules to implement the No Surprises Act, I applaud the law’s success in preventing patients from being hit with surprise medical bills in most cases.

However, a small number of out-of-network providers are using the law to extract enormous payments from health plans. This behavior is starting to drive up the cost of coverage for both employers and individuals. In my view, if left unaddressed, these increases will only get steeper.

The No Surprises Act was designed to address a troublesome feature of the U.S. healthcare system: It is notoriously difficult to predict how much your healthcare will cost. This is especially true when someone receives out-of-network care.

Before the law went into effect, roughly 20% of inpatient emergency department visits resulted in a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider. Surprise bills are common for other types of care too. One study found roughly 40% of air ambulance rides resulted in a surprise bill, costing an average of almost US$20,000.

The threat of these bills exacted an enormous emotional and financial toll. Roughly two-thirds of Americans reported being very or somewhat worried about unexpected medical bills, according to a 2020 poll conducted by KFF, a national health policy nonprofit.

The No Surprises Act protects Americans from certain instances of a practice called balance billing, in which an out-of-network hospital or doctor asks you to pay the difference between what they billed for a service and what your insurance agreed to pay for it.

When a provider joins your plan’s network, they agree to accept a specific payment for a given service or procedure. They agree to charge you only for cost sharing, such as a copayment, coinsurance or deductible, and they aren’t allowed to balance bill you.

However, plans can’t prevent out-of-network providers or facilities from balance billing. On top of that, your own plan may also charge you a higher copayment, coinsurance or deductible when you go out of network. That’s why out-of-network care can be much more expensive than in-network care.

The No Surprises Act protects consumers from these extra costs in cases where they have little or no control over whether they see an in- or out-of-network doctor. The law prohibits balance billing and requires cost sharing to be at approximately in-network levels in three cases where surprise medical bills were common:

If you receive out-of-network emergency care at a hospital or independent freestanding emergency facility. In a medical emergency, you’re not expected to figure out whether the closest hospital is in-network. You can’t be balance billed.

If an out-of-network provider treats you during a visit to an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center. For example, if an out-of-network anesthesiologist cares for you during a surgery at an in-network hospital, that anesthesiologist cannot balance bill you.
If you receive out-of-network air ambulance services.

The No Surprises Act doesn’t prevent big, unexpected medical bills in all cases. For example, you can still get balance billed for ground ambulance services or if you see an out-of-network doctor outside of a hospital or ambulatory surgical center.

The No Surprises Act is working as promised for patients – as of September 2026, it has prevented approximately 50 million surprise medical bills. But there’s a downside: Employers and unions are raising the alarm that the No Surprises Act is increasing the cost of providing health insurance.
What’s driving up costs is an arbitration process run amok.

Rather than specifying how much insurance plans should pay out-of-network providers, the law allows providers who are dissatisfied with the plan’s payment to bring disputes to arbitration. Each side submits an offer. The arbitrator must select one party’s offer as the out-of-network payment.

To choose an offer, the arbitrator considers information submitted by both parties. Information can vary by case. But the law requires the arbitrator to always consider an amount that is basically the middle amount the health plan pays in-network providers for the same service.

Health policy experts like me anticipated most disputes would be settled close to this amount. Over time, experts expected this would put downward pressure on the cost of healthcare and result in payments to both in- and out-of-network providers going down. The Congressional Budget Office predicted these lower payments would reduce premiums for consumers by 1% and reduce federal deficits by $17 billion.

As a federal employee, I worked on rules that would have required the arbitrators to treat the middle amount as a strong benchmark. I expected those rules to achieve savings like those predicted by the Congressional Budget Office. But lawsuits from providers blocked those rules from going into effect.
Without those rules, arbitrators are selecting offers that are far above what plans would pay in-network. The winning offers are also much larger than what Medicare would pay for the same service.

Providers are winning the vast majority – roughly 85% – of these disputes. They are also using arbitration more than expected. The federal government estimated there would be 17,000 disputes annually. Last year, there were more than 2 million disputes, many brought by providers with private equity investment. And the volume of disputes has grown every year.
Frequent and big provider wins at arbitration will not put downward pressure on healthcare prices. They will likely do the opposite.
When a provider wins an arbitration dispute, an individual patient’s cost sharing doesn’t change. It is capped at what the in-network amount would have been.

However, consumers as a group are the ones who ultimately will pay for the cost of arbitration. Researchers estimate the arbitration process alone cost health plans $22.4 billion in the law’s first four years. This doesn’t include the increases in in-network rates that are likely to occur if arbitration trends continue on pace.
I’m concerned that to pay for this, insurance companies will increase rates. Employers will need to budget more to pay for health insurance or increase the amount their employees pay.

We’re already seeing the costs of arbitration affect the price of health insurance. The New York state employee plan reported that the No Surprises Act was a key driver behind the plan’s 10% rate hike for 2027. A Texas city reported the No Surprises Act caused its employee plan to exceed its 2026 budget by $40 million.

Right now, only a small portion of providers use arbitration. If volume continues to grow and providers continue to win big, the cost of arbitration will grow as well – and so too will costs for consumers.
With healthcare costs a huge concern for Americans and a major issue in the 2026 midterm elections, the No Surprises Act is under scrutiny.

Congress appears interested in addressing this threat to affordability. In September 2026, the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee hosted a roundtable to discuss options to fix the law. In October, U.S. Rep. Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat, introduced legislation to scuttle the arbitration system entirely.
Absent action by Congress, I fear that the protection the No Surprises Act offers Americans will come at a cost that ultimately limits consumers’ access to health insurance.
Lindsey Murtagh receives funding from Arnold Ventures

articles.title: Is sexual objectification hard-wired? Our study used electrical brain stimulation to find out
articles.author: Ciro Civile, Associate Professor, Psychology, University of Exeter
paras: When people view sexualised images of women, they tend to remember them less well than sexualised images of men; a quirk of memory that psychologists link to objectification. But in our new study, my colleagues and I found an unlikely “fix” – applying a mild electrical current to the forehead.

Objectification means seeing someone as a body, or a set of body parts, rather than as a whole person. Our results, published in Social Neuroscience, suggest this bias in perception is not hard-wired and can be changed – at least for a while.

Psychologists measure it with an upside-down test. People are much better at recognising faces and bodies the right way up – typically about 80% right, against 55% upside down – because we take in how all the parts fit together. With objects, such as houses, turning them over matters far less, because we recognise them by their parts.

A 2012 study used this test on sexualised images. Volunteers briefly saw a photo, then had to pick it out from a pair: the photo itself and its mirror image. Men and women alike did far better with men in underwear when the photos were upright, but did about as well with women in similar poses either way – the pattern expected for objects.

The finding has been debated, and some attempts to repeat it have failed. But a 2022 analysis pooling results from 41 papers found the “upright advantage” – how much better people recognise someone the right way up than upside down – is smaller for sexualised women than sexualised men.

Sexually objectified women are seen as less competent and less fully human, and women who absorb this view of themselves tend to have poorer body image and worse mental, physical and sexual health. Exposure to sexualised media is also linked to greater tolerance of sexual violence against women.

The bias also shifts with circumstances. In a 2015 study, blurring out women’s chests and groins, or describing them as medical graduates raising money for cancer research, made people recognise their bodies more like men’s.

Power plays a part. In earlier research in Canada, a colleague and I asked people to spend ten minutes writing about a time they had power over someone, or when someone had power over them. An established way to make people feel powerful or powerless.

Women who felt powerful showed the object-like pattern for sexualised men, and powerful men showed it for sexualised women. People who felt powerless showed the upright advantage for both. Power, rather than gender itself, may be central to objectification.
Where the brain stimulation idea came from

The idea of trying brain stimulation came from my lab’s work on a famous illusion. In the Thatcher illusion, first shown with a photo of the former British prime minister, a face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks grotesque the right way up but almost normal upside down.

Turning “Thatcherised” faces upside down also hurts recognition much less than it does with ordinary faces – just as with sexualised women. We had found that the same weak current made Thatcherised faces easier to recognise the right way up, bringing back the usual difference. Would it do the same for sexualised women?

In our new study, 76 university students tried to memorise photos of male and female models posing in underwear – half of them upside down. They then saw the same photos again, each the same way up as before and mixed with 32 new ones, and said whether they had seen each one before.

Half the students received a weak current for ten minutes, using a technique called transcranial direct current stimulation. The others received a placebo that switched off after 30 seconds – a standard way of mimicking the tingle of the real thing. Neither the students nor the researchers testing them knew who got which.

The placebo group showed the familiar pattern. They remembered men far better when the photos were upright than when upside down. For women, the difference was much smaller, mainly because they remembered upright women less well than upright men.
In the stimulated group, recognition of upright images of women improved, and the gap between images of men and women disappeared. The current did not change the upright advantage for images of men.

Why? Our best explanation comes from a theory of how people learn to see. With experience, the brain learns to play down features that all faces share and to pick out the details that tell one person from another.

But some shared features grab attention instead, such as the flipped eyes and mouth of a Thatcherised face – or, we suspect, the body parts on display in sexualised images. They crowd out the details that tell one person from another. The current may weaken that pull.

Our study was a single lab session with university students, and we only measured its immediate effects, not attitudes or behaviour. Because every image was sexualised, we also cannot say how much of the gap comes from sexualisation itself rather than other differences between the photos.

Brain stimulation is no cure for sexism. But if ten minutes of a weak current – or ten minutes spent writing about feeling powerful or powerless – can shift how people see a body, objectification looks less like a fixed feature of human vision and more like a habit. And habits, unlike hard-wiring, can change.
Ciro Civile receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and previously from the European Union Horizon

articles.title: When things go bump in the night: how our brains trick us into hearing things that aren’t there
articles.author: Michelle Spear, Professor of Anatomy, University of Bristol
paras: It’s three in the morning. You’ve woken from a dead sleep because you’ve heard a thud in the darkness or a floorboard creaking downstairs. Or perhaps you’ve woken because you have the unmistakable sensation you’re not alone.
During daylight, these phenomena might be dismissed as the heating, your neighbours or the sounds of an old house settling. But in the middle of the night they can feel a tad more sinister.

Your mind might immediately start reeling, jumping to the worst case scenario – wondering if you’ve been broken into, or if you’re being haunted by some supernatural force. In reality, the explanation is far more simple. Things really do go bump in the night. But occasionally, the culprit is closer to home than we might imagine.

Falling asleep is not the neurological equivalent of switching off a light. The brain moves gradually from wakefulness into sleep, accompanied by changes in sensory processing, muscle activity and awareness of the world around us.
But these changes don’t always occur in perfect synchrony. So for brief periods, characteristics of sleep and wakefulness can overlap. The results can be surprisingly spooky.

If you’ve ever been on the verge of sleep only to feel that you’ve fallen off a kerb, missed a step or dropped through the bed, you’ve probably experienced a hypnic jerk. Also known as a sleep start, this is a sudden involuntary contraction of one or more muscles as we move into the earliest stages of sleep. It’s an example of how the transition between wakefulness and sleep isn’t always a smooth one.

Hypnagogic experiences can also involve vivid sounds, images or sensations. So as you’re on the edge of sleep, you may think you hear footsteps or whispers – or you may even think you see a figure in the room.

Exploding head syndrome – perhaps the most alarming name for a harmless sleep condition – is another example of how the boundaries between sleep and wakefulness can become blurred. As someone is falling asleep, or occasionally waking, they suddenly perceive an enormous noise: an explosion, gun shot or slamming door – yet nothing in the outside world has made a sound.
Its precise cause remains uncertain. But the phenomenon demonstrates something important: hearing a sound and a sound actually occurring are not quite the same thing.

The conscious experience of hearing is constructed by the brain. So neural activity generated without an external sound can still produce an auditory experience that seems entirely real. The brain doesn’t even need to be asleep for this to happen. If you’ve ever thought you’ve heard someone call your name – only to turn around and find no one there – you’ve been tricked by your brain.

Another possible explanation for the sounds we think we hear at night involves source monitoring. This is the brain’s ability to distinguish events generated internally from those coming from the outside world.

Thoughts, memories and imagined speech are internally generated, yet normally retain the quality of being ours. But occasionally, that attribution goes awry – allowing something generated within the brain to feel as though it came from somewhere else. Around sleep, that boundary becomes particularly interesting.
Another common – but frightening – experience that can happen at night is waking up with the sudden feeling that someone else is in the room. This experience is usually the result of sleep paralysis.

During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most of our vivid dreaming occurs, the brain temporarily suppresses activity in most muscles. This protective mechanism, known as REM atonia, prevents us from physically acting out our dreams.

But during sleep paralysis, our waking awareness returns while this physical paralysis persists. You know where you are, but cannot move. Yet elements of dream perception can remain active. This is why you may have experienced the sensation that someone – or something – is in the room with you, despite clear sensory evidence of the contrary.
One clue as to why this happens comes from experiments examining how the brain distinguishes itself from others.

In one study, participants controlled a robotic device positioned in front of them, while a second robot, which was placed behind them, reproduced these movements by touching the participants’ backs. But when researchers introduced a slight delay between the movement and the touch, some participants began to feel as though somebody else was touching them. Some even sensed another person standing behind them.

While this experiment doesn’t explain every felt presence that can happen during sleep paralysis, it does reveal something remarkable: the distinction between ourselves and others is something the brain has to construct.

Usually, movement, touch and our sense of body position agree about what belongs to us. But if that relationship is disrupted, an internally generated sensation can begin to feel like it originated elsewhere.
Now picture this happening in a dark bedroom, when you’re partly awake yet still on the edge of dreaming and unable to move. The sensation that somebody else is there becomes rather less mysterious.

Perception is not a passive recording of the world. It combines incoming sensory information with expectation and previous experience to construct the most likely explanation. But at the boundary between sleep and waking, this process can become less reliable. We may hear sounds that were never made, experience fragments of dreams intruding our bedroom or interpret sensations arising from our own bodies as the presence of somebody else.

articles.title: What brain scans can reveal, and why they don’t always explain symptoms
articles.author: Simon Keller, Professor of Neuroimaging, Pharmacology & Therapeutics, University of Liverpool
paras: In 2007, researchers in the Netherlands scanned the brains of 2,000 people aged 45 and over who were going about their ordinary lives. Seven in every 100 had signs of a stroke they never knew they’d had. Nearly two in 100 had a small bulge in a blood vessel, and a similar number had a tumour that appeared to be benign, meaning it was not cancerous.
Yet only two of those 2,000 people reported symptoms that could be linked to what the brain scanner found. Both had hearing loss.

That finding sits at the heart of how brain scans are used in medicine. A scan shows what the brain looks like but it cannot, on its own, tell you why someone is unwell. Joining those two things up is the hard part, and it is still mostly done by people rather than machines.

The most detailed pictures of the brain’s structure often come from MRI, which uses a powerful magnet and radio waves rather than X-rays. It can reveal a tumour, bleeding, the scar left by a stroke or head injury, or a patch of brain that didn’t develop quite as it should have before birth. Some of these changes are smaller than a grain of rice.

What a standard MRI can’t show is how the brain’s electrical activity changes from moment to moment. Migraine and many types of epilepsy, for example, often leave the brain looking completely normal. A clear scan is reassuring, but it doesn’t mean nothing is wrong.

How much a scan shows also depends on how it is done and who reads it. In my own field, epilepsy, a German study of 123 people being assessed for epilepsy surgery found that routine scans reported by radiologists without specialist epilepsy experience spotted only 39% of the abnormalities linked to people’s seizures. Scans done using an epilepsy-specific approach and read by specialists found 91%. Scarring in the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that can be a source of seizures, was missed in 86% of the routine reports.

Many scan reports use the word “lesion”, and people reading their own results online often find it frightening. On its own, it shouldn’t be. Lesion is a deliberately vague word that simply means an area looking different from the tissue around it.

That could be a tumour, but it could equally be an old scar or a pocket of fluid. Another common finding is small bright spots in the brain’s wiring, known as white matter lesions. In an Australian study of healthy people in their 40s, about half had at least one.

They become more common with age, and small ones often cause no obvious problems. But some are associated with changes in the brain’s small blood vessels and can be a reason to check risk factors such as high blood pressure.
So a lesion is a description, not a diagnosis. It tells a doctor where to look, not what they have found.

So how do specialists decide whether something on a scan actually explains someone’s symptoms? The first question is location. Different parts of the brain do different jobs. A scar in the area that handles vision fits with someone whose seizures start with flashing lights. The same scar in someone with tension headaches is less likely to explain their symptoms.

The second question is whether other evidence points the same way. Doctors listen closely to how the symptoms begin and unfold. They may also record the brain’s electrical activity with small sensors on the scalp or repeat the scan months later to see whether anything has changed. Something that grows is treated very differently from something that has sat still for years.

In epilepsy surgery, this matching is done formally. Neurologists, radiologists, neurosurgeons and psychologists meet to ask whether the scan, the symptoms and the electrical recordings all point to the same part of the brain. When they agree, removing that small area of tissue can stop seizures altogether in some people. When they don’t, the team may place electrodes inside the brain to pin down the source before considering an operation.
The process also works in reverse. A team may decide that a striking-looking abnormality is just a bystander and leave it alone, sparing someone an operation that would not have helped.
That is why a scan report is best read as one piece of evidence rather than a verdict. The picture matters, but only once it has been matched to the person it came from.
Simon Keller receives funding from Epilepsy Research Institute (UK), Royal Society and Pain Relief Foundation (UK).

articles.title: 1 in 4 Pennsylvanians say they paid out of pocket for their annual checkup. Why isn’t insurance covering these preventive visits?
articles.author: Sujeong Park, Assistant Professor of Health Policy and Addiction Studies, Penn State
paras: I was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing.

The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care.
Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too.

The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA.

When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero.

As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time?

Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup.
Why a preventive visit may come with a bill

Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying.

The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients.
Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free.

If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible.
Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred.

Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket.

Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year.
Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50.

After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100.
Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable.

Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate.

I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective.

Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care.

Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge.

If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision.
A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed.

Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs.

This project was supported, in part, by funding from Penn State’s Social Science Research Institute (SSRI). The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the views of SSRI or Penn State.

articles.title: Plans with cheaper premiums are risky business for Americans seeking lower healthcare costs
articles.author: Thomas Buchmueller, Professor of Business Economics and Public Policy, University of Michigan
paras: Healthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety.

Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options.

We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers.
But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive.
People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks.

Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether.

The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces.
Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape.

Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers.
Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious.
Less costly short-term plans

As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons.

First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses.

Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans.
Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states.
Alternatives that look like insurance

Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance.

Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim.

Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits.

Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture.

These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage.
Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option.

If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections.
If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself:

Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance.

If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive.

Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance.

Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be.

Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. articles.title: Private equity is buying up more methadone clinics – access to the lifesaving drug isn’t getting easier
articles.author: Yashaswini Singh, Thomas J. and Alice M. Tisch Assistant Professor of Health Services, Policy and Practice, Brown University
paras: Three times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic.

Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025.
“It’s been a godsend,” she said.
But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home.
The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m.
Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open.

That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic.
“They said they’d be at my house at 6 o'clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said.

Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it.

For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities.
Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care.

I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities.

This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety.
Why methadone fits the private equity model
Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly.

In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so.
Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply.

That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication.

Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms.

In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply.

To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator.
Market share grew, methadone supply didn’t
My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs.

Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it.

Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period.
In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed.

As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners.

Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone.

In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open.
Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units.
Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said.
No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said.

Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging.
But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens.

For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose.
A proposal to expand methadone access

These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs.
The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term.

Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027.

In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic.
“I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.”

The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk.

The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out.

Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form.

Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment.

Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug.
“We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it.

Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further.
“It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email.

The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it.
“They don’t have to die,” she said.
Bringing private equity deals into view
Two other policy responses are gaining traction.

The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies.

Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony.

The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county.

The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close.
Structural barriers to getting treatment

The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. In 2024, federal data shows the number of people who died from drug overdoses declined to nearly 80,000, and more than 54,000 of those deaths involved opioids.

We already have medications that work. The barriers preventing people from accessing them are not primarily clinical. They are structural – and, in this case, actively maintained by financial investors who profit from the status quo.
“Addiction isn’t a choice,” Titus told The Conversation.
She and her husband work for Cochise Harm Reduction, a grassroots nonprofit organization based in rural southeast Arizona that works to make life better for people who use drugs.
“It’s a learning curve and eventually … you get tired of it and you want help.”

articles.title: Your bottom shape doesn’t reveal your oestrogen levels – despite what social media says
articles.author: Adam Taylor, Professor of Anatomy, Lancaster University
paras: The shape of your bottom cannot tell you anything about your hormones, whatever recent social media posts claim. The only way to find out your levels of cortisol, oestrogen or anything else is a blood test.

A heart-shaped bottom, influencers say, signals healthy oestrogen, while an H shape means too much cortisol. In reality, buttock shape doesn’t reflect your circulating hormone levels from day to day, week to week or month to month.

So what decides your shape? Mostly your genes. They give you your skeletal structure and your muscle size and structure. And in the buttocks and everywhere else, how much fat you are likely to carry there.

The shape of the pelvis varies between people. In obstetrics, four traditional categories describe the internal bony structure of the pelvis, which is also the shape of the opening through which a baby passes during birth: gynaecoid, android, anthropoid and platypelloid.

Gynaecoid is the most common in females and the most favourable for a vaginal birth. Android is narrower and close to the shape of a male pelvis. Anthropoid is narrower from side to side but longer from front to back, while platypelloid is the reverse. You cannot tell which type a woman has by looking at the skin over her pelvis or buttocks.

This bony framework is what your muscles attach to. It also decides the spaces around them that get filled in with fat. Almost all the features you can see or measure on your hips and buttocks come from this bony architecture. In other words, your skeleton sets the starting point.
Over the top sits the skin, which shows the contours of the tissue underneath. This gives rise to the buttock types often described by plastic surgeons: H-, A-, O- and inverted V-shaped.

The crease beneath each buttock, known as the infragluteal fold, forms where the skin and underlying tissues are attached to deeper structures. These attachments help determine the position and shape of the lower edge of the buttocks.

Muscle also contributes to the shape of the buttocks, and it’s the part you can change most easily. Some people who lose a substantial amount of weight while taking GLP-1 medicines develop what is known as “Ozempic butt”, in which the buttocks appear flatter or more sagging. This can reflect the loss of fat and muscle, as well as changes in the skin.

Buttock shape does change later in life for women. This is typically linked to the menopause, when levels of oestrogen begin to decline. As oestrogen falls, fat is deposited towards the abdomen rather than under the skin around the hips and buttocks, as it is before menopause. So hormones do shape where fat goes, but only as part of a slow, long-term change.

This does not mean a woman will move from one buttock shape to another – genetics do not change. Any short-term change across the menstrual cycle, driven by hormone rhythms, is likely to be unnoticeable. It would be down to fluid retention, which happens across the whole body rather than in one specific region.
A woman’s skeleton also alters with ageing around the menopause, influenced by muscle loss, changing hormones and looser connective tissues. But this is a long-term process.

Stress will not change things either. A particularly stressful period will shift your cortisol levels, but this will not make fat move from your bum to your tum. Stress might cause more fat to be stored in one area, but it is well recognised that our genetics determine where our fat is stored.

This is not the first time social media has tried to convince people that their buttock shape can be changed. Hip dips have also been suggested as something you can modify, but like the buttocks, their shape is mainly influenced by genetics, which drive our skeletal and muscular structure.
Changing anything so reliant on genetics often takes surgery. And in this part of the body, certain operations carry some of the highest risks of death from cosmetic surgery.

Your buttock shape reflects a combination of inherited anatomy, fat and muscle. Hormones can influence how that shape changes over time, particularly around menopause, but appearance alone cannot tell you whether your hormone levels are normal.

articles.title: Exercise can sometimes cause chest pain – and this condition may be to blame
articles.author: Helen Rainford, Lead for Primary Care, School of Medicine and Dentistry, University of Lancashire
paras: As a GP, I know that chest pain is one symptom that makes people worry. The immediate concern is that it’s a sign there’s something seriously wrong – such as a problem with their heart or lungs.

But these aren’t the only reasons that chest pain can happen. For many otherwise healthy people, especially those who exercise regularly, the sudden onset of chest pain may actually be caused by a painful, yet generally harmless, condition called costochondritis.

Costochondritis occurs when the tissue connecting the ribs to the breastbone becomes irritated. This causes pain at the front of the chest, usually close to the breastbone. Patients describe the pain as sharp, aching or sore, and it’s often aggravated by stretching, twisting, exercise, coughing or taking a deep breath. The area is frequently tender to touch and pressing on it can cause pain.
Costochondritis is thought to be the cause of approximately 13% of GP visits for chest pain. The condition is diagnosed based on a person’s symptoms and examination.

There’s no specific blood test or scan that can confirm costochondritis. Instead, the diagnosis is usually based on a person’s symptoms and a physical examination. However, tests such as an electrocardiogram (ECG), which records the heart’s electrical activity, or a chest x-ray may sometimes be needed to rule out more serious issues. This is particularly important in people aged over 35 years and those with a history of, or risk factors for, coronary heart disease.
What causes costochondritis?
The exact causes of costochondritis aren’t always clear. It’s often linked to strain affecting the area where the ribs join the breastbone.

For many people, the condition is triggered by repetitive physical activity or overuse of the upper body. Weight training, rowing, heavy lifting or exercises involving repeated pushing and pulling movements can place extra stress on the chest wall.

The risk appears to be greatest when exercise intensity increases too quickly. A sudden jump in training volume, frequency or the weight a person is lifting can overload tissues that haven’t had time to adapt.

Costochondritis can also happen after a minor chest injury – such as a fall or a blow sustained during contact sports. Another common trigger is persistent coughing. This places considerable strain on the chest wall’s muscles and tissues, which is why some people develop costochondritis during or after a heavy cold or chest infection.

Understanding what triggered costochondritis is an important part of recovery. Most cases improve with simple self-care measures. The first step is usually trying to temporarily avoid or reduce the activities that provoked the pain – particularly heavy lifting and repetitive upper-body exercise. You should avoid these activities until the pain settles.

Anti-inflammatory pain medicines, such as paracetamol and ibuprofen, can also help reduce symptoms where suitable. Many people also find that applying a heat pack or warm compress helps ease discomfort.

As symptoms begin to settle, gentle chest, shoulder and upper back stretches can help improve mobility and prevent stiffness. For instance, the thoracic extension exercise, in which a person stretches their back over a low chair while their hands are placed behind their head, showed benefit for some patients.
Costochondritis often improves on its own. Symptoms may last for a several weeks or several months, but most people make a full recovery within a year.
Can costochondritis be prevented?

It’s not always possible to prevent costochondritis, but a few sensible precautions can reduce the risk. If you’re starting a new exercise programme or increasing your weights, build up gradually and give your body time to adapt. Good lifting technique, whether in the gym or at work, can also reduce unnecessary strain on the chest wall.

It’s also important to avoid overtraining. Exercising too hard, too often or without adequate recovery increases the risk of overuse injuries, including costochondritis. Rest days are not a sign of weakness; they are part of training.
Don’t forget stretching. Regular stretching can also help maintain flexibility and mobility in the chest, shoulders and upper back.

Most importantly, don’t ignore pain. If your chest wall starts hurting during exercise, resist the temptation to push through it. Continuing to strain irritated tissues can prolong symptoms and delay recovery.

Costochondritis can be painful and worrying, but it’s usually not a serious condition. Just make sure you don’t dismiss any chest pain you’re experiencing or assume it’s costochondritis. This is especially key if your chest pain is severe, feels tight or heavy, or the pain spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back. Similarly seek medical advice if the pain is accompanied by other symptoms – such as shortness of breath, nausea, sweating or dizziness.
Once more serious causes have been excluded, most people recover fully with a combination of rest, a gradual return to activity and sensible exercise habits.

articles.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
articles.author: Andrés Henao, Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild.
As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick.

A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor.

Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year.
Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship.

Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year, and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China. Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak. And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world.

In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis, often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong.
Let your itinerary guide the conversation
Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks.

Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia.
What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards.

So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital.
Illnesses you can safely treat yourself

For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference.

Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide, an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea.

When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them.

The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch. A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents.
Build a small medical kit – not a portable pharmacy

A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts, loperamide, antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip.

People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names.

Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning.
Be skeptical of popular travel remedies

Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results. Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos. And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea, as their efficacy is still unknown.

Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “Natural” does not mean effective, or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug.
Ask about when to seek medical care
Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate.

Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip.

At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe altitude illness is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute.

Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface weeks or even months after you get home, which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked.

I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care?
International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.
